reference_proof: Compute the difference: $\left|\dfrac{3n-1}{n+2}-3\right|=\left|\dfrac{3n-1-3(n+2)}{n+2}\right|=\dfrac{7}{n+2}<\dfrac{7}{n}$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, by the Archimedean property take a positive integer $N>\dfrac{7}{\varepsilon}$. Then for $n\ge N$, $\dfrac{7}{n}\le\dfrac{7}{N}<\varepsilon$, so $\left|\dfrac{3n-1}{n+2}-3\right|<\varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$

statement: Prove that $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$ is not uniformly continuous on $(0,1)$.
reference_proof: Take $\varepsilon_0=1$. Let $x_n=\dfrac1n$ and $y_n=\dfrac1{n+1}$ (both in $(0,1)$). Then $|x_n-y_n|=\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)}\to0$, which can be made smaller than any $\delta$; but $|f(x_n)-f(y_n)|=|n-(n+1)|=1\ge\varepsilon_0$. So there exists $\varepsilon_0$ such that for every $\delta$ a counterexample can be found — not uniformly continuous. (Root cause: $f'$ is unbounded near $0$.) $\blacksquare$

statement: Suppose $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ and $f(q)=0$ for every rational $q$. Prove that $f\equiv0$.
reference_proof: Take any real $a$. Since the rationals are dense in $\mathbb{R}$, there is a sequence of rationals $q_n\to a$. By continuity of $f$ at $a$ (sequential criterion), $f(a)=\lim_{n\to\infty}f(q_n)$. But each $f(q_n)=0$, so $f(a)=0$. As $a$ was arbitrary, $f\equiv0$. $\blacksquare$

statement: Suppose $f$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ with $|f'(x)|\le M$. Prove that $f$ is uniformly continuous.
reference_proof: If $M=0$ then $f$ is constant, obviously uniformly continuous. Suppose $M>0$. Take any $x,y$; by the Lagrange mean value theorem there is $c$ with $f(x)-f(y)=f'(c)(x-y)$, so $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M|x-y|$ (Lipschitz). Given $\varepsilon>0$, take $\delta=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{M}$ (independent of the point). Then $|x-y|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$: uniformly continuous. $\blacksquare$

statement: Using the mean value theorem, prove that $e^x>1+x$ for all $x>0$.
reference_proof: Let $f(t)=e^t$, continuous on $[0,x]$ and differentiable on $(0,x)$, with $f'(t)=e^t$. By the Lagrange mean value theorem there is $c\in(0,x)$ with $e^x-e^0=e^c(x-0)$, i.e. $e^x-1=e^c x$. Since $c>0$, $e^c>1$, and $x>0$, so $e^x-1=e^c x>x$, i.e. $e^x>1+x$. $\blacksquare$

On $[0,1]$, $1\le1+x$, so $0\le\dfrac{x^n}{1+x}\le x^n$. Monotonicity of the integral gives $0\le\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x^n}{1+x}\,dx\le\int_0^1 x^n\,dx=\dfrac{1}{n+1}$. As $n\to\infty$, $\dfrac{1}{n+1}\to0$, so by the squeeze theorem the integral limit is $0$. $\blacksquare$

statement: Use the comparison test to prove that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\dfrac{1}{n^2+1}$ converges.
reference_proof: For every $n\ge1$, $n^2+1>n^2>0$, so $0<\dfrac{1}{n^2+1}<\dfrac{1}{n^2}$. It is known that $\sum\dfrac{1}{n^2}$ converges ($p=2>1$). By the comparison test ($0\le a_n\le b_n$ with $\sum b_n$ convergent implies $\sum a_n$ convergent), $\sum\dfrac{1}{n^2+1}$ converges. $\blacksquare$

statement: Use the ratio test to prove that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\dfrac{n}{2^n}$ converges.
reference_proof: Let $a_n=\dfrac{n}{2^n}>0$. The ratio $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{(n+1)/2^{n+1}}{n/2^n}=\dfrac{n+1}{2n}=\dfrac12\Big(1+\dfrac1n\Big)\to\dfrac12$. Since the limit $\dfrac12<1$, by the ratio test $\sum\dfrac{n}{2^n}$ converges absolutely. $\blacksquare$
